criteria.note: The keyword intent ('is tteok gluten free') is answered inside the first ~160 words — 'There wasn't — in this one' plus the immediate 밀떡 correction — and the first two H2s complete the rule.
Title is 38 chars + 20 for the appended suffix = 58 (<=60), keyword present as 'Gluten-Free Tteok', description ~145 chars, and the description adds the 밀떡 angle rather than restating the title.

Headings assert rather than label — a skim of 'glutinous rice has no gluten' → 'But not all tteok is rice: 밀떡' → 'The moment the math stopped working' → 'Making it at home' delivers the argument without the body.
Four distinct internal destinations (hidden-gluten guide, Monil2 House, celiac travel guide, related-guides block), each placed where the reader would actually want the next step.

All three FAQ answers — the 밀떡/소맥분 label check, the GIG-sourced glutinous-rice point, and the butter tteok recipe-vs-kitchen distinction — are established in the body and each reads standalone as a rich result.
Concrete but thin: a real price observation and a home batch, but no named shop, no purchase date, no measured quantities for the thing the author says he made.
criteria.evidence_quote: I'm not going to hand you exact gram-by-gram ratios, because I worked mostly by feel and I'd rather not invent precision I didn't measure.

criteria.note: Korean terms are consistently romanised (찹쌀가루 chapssal-garu, 밀떡 mil-tteok, 쌀떡 ssal-tteok, 타피오카 전분 tapioka jeonbun), the label terms to scan for are named (밀, 소맥분, 같은 제조시설), and prices are exact.

Two primary sources are linked (Gluten Intolerance Group, 식품등의 표시기준) but both carry only a retrieval date, not a publication or amendment date, so a reader cannot tell which version of the standard is being described.

The piece names what its method cannot establish — the anecdote disclaimer, the 'blank line is weaker evidence' caveat, the 'dedicated is the operator's claim' note — and openly withdraws an unverifiable No Brand claim; no commercial links present.

findings.quote: Korea's [식품등의 표시기준](https://www.law.go.kr/행정규칙/식품등의표시기준) does require that caution line where a designated allergen may unavoidably carry over from a shared process (retrieved August 2026)
findings.why: A regulatory standard is amended repeatedly; a retrieval date tells the reader when the author looked, not which version of the rule they are relying on. Same gap on the Gluten Intolerance Group citation.
findings.fix: Add the notice/amendment number and date for 식품등의 표시기준 (e.g. 식약처 고시 제20XX-XX호, DD Month YYYY) alongside the retrieval date, and give the GIG page's published or last-updated date if the page shows one.

findings.quote: Around **6,000 won for three pieces, plus another 500 won to add condensed milk.**
findings.why: This is the article's strongest first-hand detail but it floats free of a place and a date, so a reader cannot situate or check it — the difference between an observation and a generic price anecdote.
findings.fix: Name the cafe (or at least neighbourhood and month of purchase) next to the price, and add one or two specifics from the home batch — mold size, number of pieces yielded, or what failed on the first attempt.

findings.quote: <!-- IMG: 01.webp — homemade butter tteok, first batch, top-down on a plate. Caption: "Our first home batch — not bad at all." -->
findings.why: The only visual evidence of the home batch ships as an HTML comment, so it renders as nothing — the reader loses the proof-of-experience image and the page loses an indexable asset with alt text.
findings.fix: Replace the comment with the actual image element pointing at the optimised webp, with descriptive alt text and the intended caption.

findings.quote: where the danger is [hidden in the sauce or the batter](/blog/hidden-gluten-korean-food)
findings.why: The hidden-gluten guide is linked three times in the body plus once in the related-guides block; the second and third instances add no new destination and dilute the anchor signal.
findings.fix: Keep the tteokbokki-context link and the related-guides entry, and either drop the middle repeat or point it at a different relevant page (e.g. the 쌀빵 claim could link to a rice-bread or label-reading piece).

criteria.note: The two load-bearing claims (glutinous rice, Korea's shared-facility labelling duty) are properly sourced and the price/recipe details are marked as the author's own experience, but a handful of category-level assertions about wheat in tteokbokki components and cafe kitchens carry no source.
criteria.evidence_quote: the sauce is gochujang (usually wheat) and the fish cake mixed in is typically bound with wheat starch

criteria.note: Product and place names are checkable, the one unverifiable product claim was explicitly withdrawn rather than kept, and the prices, dates and retrieval notes are internally consistent.

The piece states how it knows (retrieved sources with dates, a failed re-verification, cooking done by feel) and is explicit that an ingredient list cannot establish celiac safety, with no keyword match dressed up as ingredient analysis.

No absolute clearance is given, cross-contamination is addressed at both the kitchen and the milling stage, the NCGS/celiac line is drawn explicitly, and the 'she felt fine' anecdote is pre-emptively disarmed with asymptomatic damage.
Both external sources carry a 'retrieved August 2026' stamp and the piece flags that Korean reformulation and cafe recipes make all of it perishable rather than a standing clearance.

Korean terms (찹쌀가루, 밀떡/쌀떡, 소맥분, 타피오카 전분, 같은 제조시설) are used correctly and the load-bearing labelling fact is stated exactly right — the duty covers 밀 but not 보리 or 호밀, with the 'unavoidable' judgement left to the maker.
The reader is told precisely what to look for on a package (밀, 소맥분 in 원재료명; a 같은 제조시설 line), given direct links to the GIG FAQ and the 식품등의 표시기준, and invited to send a correction with a photo.

findings.quote: the sauce is gochujang (usually wheat) and the fish cake mixed in is typically bound with wheat starch
findings.why: Three separate category claims carry no citation: that gochujang usually contains wheat, that fish cake is typically bound with wheat starch, and (elsewhere) that 밀떡 is a mainstream supermarket product standard at many street stalls. All three point readers away from gluten rather than toward it, so no one gets hurt acting on them, but the article's own standard elsewhere is to source or attribute, and these are the claims a reader uses to decide whether to eat tteokbokki at all.
findings.fix: Attach a source to each — a manufacturer ingredient panel photo for a named gochujang and a named 어묵, and a retailer listing or product page for a 밀떡 SKU — or mark them explicitly as the authors' repeated observation on Korean shelves, in the same voice used for the receipt and the home batch.

findings.quote: The core of it is just:
findings.why: The four-ingredient base is the factual spine of the whole piece, and its provenance is never stated. It is not attributed to a shop's ingredient panel, a named recipe, or the authors' own kitchen. The article is careful to say a shop's version may differ, which mitigates the risk, but a reader cannot tell whether this list came from a label, a blog recipe, or inference.
findings.fix: Add one clause naming where the list came from — e.g. 'the recipe we made at home, and the base every version we've seen shares' — so the reader knows whether they are reading a label or a reconstruction.

findings.quote: Most places selling butter tteok also bake wheat pastries, on the same counters and trays.
findings.why: Stated as a surveyed fact about the trade with a quantifier ('Most') and a specific mechanism ('same counters and trays'), but nothing indicates how many shops were looked at or whether kitchens were actually observed. The direction is protective, so it is not a safety hazard, but the specificity implies fieldwork the piece does not claim to have done.
findings.fix: Soften to the observed basis — 'every cafe we've seen selling it also bakes wheat pastries' — or state how many shops that judgement rests on.
